ideas.title: Proof Sketch Animator
ideas.summary: Type a plain-English description of any algorithm and watch Claude generate a step-by-step animated visualization on a live canvas. No D3 expertise required - educators get custom algorithm animations in seconds for lectures or study guides.
ideas.description: Most algorithm visualization tools require you to pick from a fixed library of pre-built animations. Proof Sketch Animator flips this: you describe what you want ('sort these five numbers by repeatedly finding the minimum and swapping it to the front') and Claude generates a structured JSON trace of states that a React renderer plays back as a smooth animation. Each step is labeled with the operation name and a one-sentence natural-language explanation. Instructors can export the animation as a standalone HTML page for lecture slides or student handouts. A preset library covers common CS1/CS2 topics so you can demo in one click without typing anything.
keyFeatures: Freeform description input: describe any algorithm in plain English and get an animated trace
Preset library for 12 common CS algorithms (bubble sort, binary search, Dijkstra, merge sort, BFS, DFS, and more)
Side-by-side panel showing the current step's pseudocode line highlighted alongside the live canvas
Step-by-step mode (click to advance) and auto-play mode with speed control
Export as a self-contained HTML page suitable for embedding in course slides
ideas.techStack: React + Vite, Tailwind CSS, Claude API (structured JSON output for trace generation), HTML5 Canvas for animation rendering, no backend required
ideas.whyInteresting: The gap between 'I want to visualize this algorithm' and 'I have a polished D3 animation' is currently measured in hours. Proof Sketch Animator collapses it to seconds, making custom algorithm visualization accessible to instructors who can explain an algorithm perfectly but have no time to code a bespoke animation.
ideas.inspiredBy: Reddit r/learnprogramming threads requesting better custom algorithm visualizations; gap between what educators can describe verbally and what they can animate without coding

ideas.title: TA Queue Intelligence
ideas.summary: An office hours queue where students describe their problem on joining and an LLM clusters similar questions in real time, letting TAs spot that eight students have the same off-by-one error and address it as a batch rather than repeating the same hint eight times.
ideas.description: Standard office hours queues (OHQueue, Queuestatus) tell a TA who is next but give no signal about what patterns are emerging across the room. TA Queue Intelligence adds an LLM categorization layer: when a student joins the queue they type a free-text problem description, which Claude classifies by error type (compilation error, logic bug, requirements misunderstanding, design question, environment setup) and by topic (linked lists, recursion, file I/O, etc.). The TA dashboard shows a live cluster view: instead of a flat list of names, they see groups like 'Null pointer on linked list insert (6 students)' with a summary hint pre-generated by Claude. TAs can broadcast a hint to all students in a cluster, mark a cluster resolved, or pull individual students into the queue normally. Post-session analytics show which topics generated the most confusion each week.
keyFeatures: Student join form with free-text problem description; no category pre-selection required
Real-time LLM clustering into error type and topic with confidence scores
TA cluster dashboard: grouped card view with student count, cluster summary, and a pre-drafted hint
Broadcast hint to a whole cluster or pull individuals into a 1:1 slot
Post-session heatmap showing confusion hotspots by topic and week for instructor review
ideas.techStack: React + Vite (student join UI + TA dashboard), Flask (queue API + LLM calls), Supabase (realtime queue state), Claude API (classification + hint generation), Tailwind CSS
ideas.whyInteresting: Office hours are structurally inefficient: instructors repeat themselves because they have no mechanism to see that the same confusion is queued 10 times. TA Queue Intelligence turns the queue into a live signal about what the class doesn't understand, shifting TAs from reactive answer-givers to proactive pattern-recognizers.
ideas.inspiredBy: Repeated observation that TAs give the same hint verbatim to 8 consecutive students during office hours; GitHub issues on OHQueue requesting analytics

ideas.title: Debugging Theater
ideas.summary: Students debug a broken program not by reading the code but by interviewing an AI character who can only describe what they observe as a user - no root cause, no stack traces - forcing systematic hypothesis-driven diagnosis as a transferable professional skill.
ideas.description: Junior developers often debug by guessing or adding print statements until something changes; they lack systematic diagnostic skill because assignments always give them the code. Debugging Theater removes the code. Students are told that a program has a bug and given a behavioral spec ('the app should accept a CSV and return a sorted list; something is wrong'). They interview an AI 'user persona' through a chat interface: the AI can respond to specific test inputs ('what happens if the first column is empty?'), describe observed behavior in plain English, and confirm or deny hypotheses ('is the output ever sorted partially?'), but is strictly constrained from revealing implementation details or error messages. Students must form a written hypothesis, test it through conversation, and submit a bug report. The instructor panel shows a log of every student's conversation and hypothesis chain, making it easy to grade diagnostic reasoning quality rather than just the correct answer. Multiple bug scenarios are provided, from off-by-one errors to race conditions, each with a different AI persona.
keyFeatures: Student chat interface with an AI user persona constrained to describe symptoms only, never source code
Structured submission form: hypothesis, supporting evidence from conversation, proposed fix
Instructor scenario builder: define a bug, the program's expected behavior, and the AI persona's allowed knowledge
Instructor review panel: full conversation logs, hypothesis chain, and scoring rubric integration
Five starter scenarios spanning CS1-CS2 topics (sorting, file parsing, linked list, recursive descent, concurrency)
ideas.techStack: React + Vite (student chat UI + instructor dashboard), Flask (conversation API with constrained system prompt), Claude API (AI user persona with behavior constraints), Supabase (conversation and submission storage), Tailwind CSS
ideas.whyInteresting: Diagnostic reasoning - the ability to narrow a hypothesis space through targeted questioning - is one of the most valued and hardest-to-teach software engineering skills. Traditional debugging assignments skip it by giving students the source code; Debugging Theater forces students to practice the exact skill that distinguishes senior engineers: knowing what question to ask next.
ideas.inspiredBy: Rubber duck debugging pedagogy; medical education case studies where students diagnose without seeing test results upfront; HN discussion on 'why new grads can't debug without print statements'

ideas.title: In-Class Snapshot Profiling for LLM-Personalized Practice in CS Courses
ideas.summary: A classroom study that replicates and extends automated student-profile detection from in-class code snapshots to an undergraduate CS2 context, then tests whether LLM-generated personalized exercises derived from each student's snapshot trajectory improve exam outcomes relative to generic practice materials.
ideas.description: Yusuf et al. (SIGCSE TS 2026) demonstrated that capturing student code snapshots every 20 seconds during in-class exercises reveals three stable behavioral profiles - Early Birds, Active Strugglers, and Delayed/Disengaged students - that emerge within the first six weeks and strongly predict exam performance (r = -0.68 between exercise access delay and midterm scores). Their LLM-generated personalized practice materials produced a striking result: 81.8% of supported students reached high-performer status. This research replicates and extends that study in two directions. First, it transfers the profiling methodology to an undergraduate CSS342 (Data Structures) context at UW, testing whether the three-profile structure holds for undergraduates versus the graduate population (n=57) in the original study. Second, it runs a controlled experiment comparing three intervention conditions: (A) no practice materials, (B) generic practice problems from the course textbook, and (C) LLM-generated exercises derived from each student's snapshot trajectory. The primary outcome is exam performance; secondary outcomes include time-on-task during subsequent in-class exercises and student self-reported confidence. The snapshot infrastructure integrates with Pisan's existing Jolly Feedback autograder, which already logs submission events, minimizing new instrumentation work. The LLM exercise generation uses Claude to analyze snapshot patterns - specifically what the student attempted, where they stalled, and which errors appeared - and produce three targeted practice problems that address their observed gaps without simply restating the original exercise.

papers.title: Using In-Class Exercise Data for Early Support of Struggling Students
papers.authors: University of Memphis (authors not listed individually in proceedings metadata)
papers.abstract: This classroom experience report investigates how in-class programming exercises can function as early-warning systems for struggling students. We studied two graduate Computer Science courses (n=57) where students' code was automatically captured every 20 seconds during short programming activities. Clustering analysis revealed three consistent profiles: Early Birds (44.4%), Active Strugglers (33.3%), and Delayed/Disengaged students (22.2%). These profiles strongly predicted exam performance (r=-0.68). LLMs were used to analyze code snapshots and generate tailored exercises; 81.8% of the 11 supported students achieved high-performer status.
papers.relevance: This paper is the direct anchor: its snapshot-capture methodology, three-profile clustering result, and LLM-exercise-generation pipeline are the components this research replicates, transfers to an undergraduate context, and evaluates with an experimental design that the original experience report does not include.

additionalRefs.title: Beyond One-Size-Fits-All Exercises: Personalizing Computer Science Worksheets with Large Language Models
additionalRefs.relevance: Demonstrates that LLMs can generate pedagogically valid, course-aligned CS exercises that adapt to learner profiles, providing methodological grounding for the exercise-generation arm of this research and a comparison baseline for evaluating generated exercise quality.

additionalRefs.title: When to Check In?: Identifying Early Signs of Student Struggle in CS Courses
additionalRefs.relevance: A complementary 2026 study that identifies early struggle indicators from a different behavioral signal (help-seeking timing and patterns), situating the snapshot-profiling approach within the broader early warning systems literature and offering a comparison signal for triangulation.

additionalRefs.title: Jolly Feedback: Automated Feedback for Programming Assignments
additionalRefs.relevance: Pisan's existing autograder infrastructure that already captures submission events and test results; extending it to capture in-class snapshot events avoids building a new logging system and ensures continuity with the lab's established data pipeline.

researchPlan.overview: The study proceeds in two phases: a replication and profiling phase (months 1-3) that instruments CSS342 with snapshot capture and validates the three-profile clustering in an undergraduate context, and a randomized comparison phase (months 4-6) that assigns struggling students to one of three practice-material conditions and measures exam outcomes. Both phases use the existing Jolly Feedback infrastructure for submission logging, minimizing new software development.

milestones.deliverable: Snapshot capture module integrated with Jolly Feedback (logging code state every 20 seconds during designated in-class exercises); IRB protocol submitted for CSS342 data collection

Cluster analysis on first six weeks of CSS342 snapshot data; comparison of undergraduate cluster structure against the original graduate three-profile model; preliminary report on whether Early Bird / Active Struggler / Delayed profiles replicate

milestones.goal: Exercise generation pipeline and quality evaluation
milestones.deliverable: Prompt templates for Claude-generated exercises conditioned on snapshot trajectory; blind expert review of 30 generated exercises for technical accuracy and pedagogical alignment; iteration on prompts based on reviewer feedback

milestones.goal: Randomized assignment of interventions to struggling students
milestones.deliverable: Students classified as Active Strugglers or Delayed/Disengaged randomly assigned to conditions A (no supplement), B (textbook problems), or C (LLM-personalized exercises); materials delivered by week 4 of the quarter

milestones.goal: Data collection: midterm outcomes and behavioral follow-up
milestones.deliverable: Midterm exam scores by condition; snapshot engagement metrics for weeks 7-10; student self-efficacy survey; preliminary between-condition comparison

Statistical comparison of exam outcomes across conditions; qualitative analysis of snapshot trajectories for representative students from each profile; submitted paper draft targeting SIGCSE TS or ICER

researchPlan.resources: Jolly Feedback autograder (existing, requires snapshot-logging extension); Claude API at Haiku tier for exercise generation (estimated $5-15 per course section per quarter); one student RA for snapshot module integration and data pipeline work; CSS342 course enrollment (typically 30-60 students per section); IRB approval for educational research under existing course evaluation protocol

risks.risk: The three-profile clustering may not replicate cleanly in an undergraduate context - profiles could be more diffuse or require more than six weeks to stabilize
risks.mitigation: Use the original paper's clustering approach (k-means on exercise access delay and problem completion rate) but also try hierarchical clustering; report both; if profiles don't replicate, reframe as a finding about population differences between graduate and undergraduate CS students

risks.risk: Sample size for the intervention arms may be too small if only 22% of students fall into Delayed/Disengaged and another 33% into Active Struggler profiles in a 40-student section
risks.mitigation: Pre-register a power analysis; if the single-section sample is insufficient, recruit one additional CSS342 section taught by a collaborating instructor; alternatively, collapse Active Strugglers and Delayed/Disengaged into a single 'at-risk' group to increase power

risks.risk: LLM-generated exercises may not be sufficiently targeted to a student's specific snapshot gaps, reducing the theoretical advantage of condition C over condition B
risks.mitigation: Include the actual code snapshots (with timestamps) in the prompt rather than just a profile label; conduct a pre-deployment expert review pass; add a student feedback loop where students rate whether the exercise felt relevant to their actual struggle
